utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Matkovic. Good afternoon, Mr. Matkovic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We will now continue with cross-examination by the Prosecution, and on this occasion you will be asked questions by Mr. Stamp. Mr. Stamp. And, sorry, just one other thing. I should remind you that the solemn declaration you made yesterday to speak the truth in your evidence continues to apply to your evidence today. Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Matkovic.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MATKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yesterday you were shown a document which is a record of the operations in the departmental staff for the suppression of terrorism in Kosovo, meeting of the 29th of October, 1998.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And that, Your Honours, is P2216.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And you saw that it is recorded there that many people at that meeting, including Mr. Milosevic, Mr. Milutinovic, Mr. Sainovic, Mr. Minic, used the term "Joint Command." Do you recall hearing any of them or anybody using that term in that meeting?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MATKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yesterday after this session I tried to think back. I tried to recall that meeting. As far as I remember, the meeting did, indeed, take place. In a way, this was the last meeting with President Milosevic in relation to what was going on in Kosovo. May I continue, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Just a minute, I'm not getting a clear -- can you hold, please, Mr. Matkovic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Certainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I'm getting a lot of feedback. I'm not hearing what is being said very well. Yes, it's still there. Is there another -- do you have another one of these.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Mr. Matkovic, can you hear me?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MATKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Matkovic. I think we are fine now. You were saying that you --

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MATKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm glad it's fine. May I repeat what I said?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: No, no, I can read it. Thank you very much. You recall the meeting. Do you recall what is recorded in the minutes? Do you recall --

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MATKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I tried to recall yesterday after my testimony, and I think this was the last meeting in the office of President Milosevic after what had happened in Kosovo, and we never met again in that same composition.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well --

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MATKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course I'm telling you everything based on my memory and on my knowledge.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well. Now --

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MATKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And I can't remember that anyone used terms like the "Joint Command" at that meeting. Needless to say, I would like to add a thing or two about that; however, it's your show. If you want to continue with your questions, please fire away.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You also attended meetings on a daily basis in Kosovo in 1998. Did you hear anybody at any of those meetings use a term "Joint Command"?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MATKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I explained yesterday, first of all, that those meetings did not take place on a daily basis. They were frequent, sometimes daily. Secondly, that term was not an official term. If someone used it- and I explained yesterday that as far as I could remember -- I had heard it used by a military man, somewhere because it is a police, a military term, but we did not use that as an official term, it's not a term that we agreed on. It's not a term that we used --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes, but --

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MATKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Therefore, wherever I happened to be, at whichever meeting, that term was not used in an official manner. Please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes, I understand that. Whether it was used officially or unofficially, all I'm asking you is: Did you hear the term used in the meeting, in any of those meetings in Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MATKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I said yesterday, didn't I, that I had heard of the term, but that term wasn't used in the sense of being used continuously. If someone used it, if one comes across that term in one of these documents westbound as someone using the term "Joint Command," then this is their own business, they used it and that's that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Matkovic, I'm stopping you there. The question is very simple: Did you hear that expression being used in any of the meetings you attended, yes or no?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very rarely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: On the occasions you heard it being used in those meetings, can you remember who used it?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MATKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I can't. The term was used very often and it wasn't an official term. There is something that I wish to point out again just in order to clarify my view, my experience, and the truth that I was facing at the time as well as the Working Group, the SPS Working Group, the people I was with. This term "Joint Command," anywhere in the world would imply some form of organisation, a command post, a command being exercised, a commander being there --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Matkovic, I'm stopping you again. You're not answering the question that you were asked. You've now said that this expression was used very often. Will you now tell us where it was used very often. Never mind whether it was official or not official, you've made your point repeatedly about that. Just tell us where it was used very often.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I said that I had heard the term used very rarely, and I think it was in an informal context but certainly not at any of the official meetings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And I was just trying to explain what this means, the Joint Command, but wherever I was, with the SPS team, the term was not used and I think I was crystal clear about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, I will ask if anyone was listening in court in Serbian to what was said in the answer at line 17 of page 4 and whether the witness said "very often" or "very rarely" at that stage. Can anyone help me on that?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, this point in time that you're referring to, he did say "very often" indeed but before that he did say "very rarely," so that may be --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Matkovic, your idea of what is crystal clear is entirely different from mine. You've said "very rarely" and you've said "very often." Please bear in mind that that is a very confusing situation for us. Can you clarify it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Your Honour, it was your question that I answered in the most direct manner possible, very rarely. I abide by that. If I used the term "very often," then it was a slip of the tongue on my part and please accept my apologies. I would like to tell you the following: According to my information and based on where all the occasions where I was physically present, there was no such thing as the Joint Command, and I hope this clarifies it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Matkovic, I understand what you are saying. All I'm asking about is the use of the term. Now, I understand you to be saying that you heard the term being used very rarely and you answered earlier that you heard it being used very rarely in the meetings that I was asking you about. And later on you seem to be saying that it was not used in the meetings. I'd like to clarify that. You said that it was used very rarely in the meetings that you attended in 1998; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MATKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, very rarely.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Now --

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MATKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And I --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: -- Can you recall --

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MATKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- Can't remember the term being used -- what?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Can you recall who used it in those meetings that you attended in 1998?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MATKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember who used the term. I don't remember anyone using that term. I said I only heard it in informal situations and, above all, from military officials.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: When you heard it being used very rarely, as you put it, at the meetings that you attended, do you know what it was referring to, what it meant when you heard it being used in those meetings?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MATKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I heard it in informal communication, this was something associated in my mind with the military or police. As for the meetings that I attended those were working meetings to pass on information. It was about coordination. It certainly didn't involve anything such as a command or the exercise of command in general.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: If you're moving on I want to ask. What do you mean by the answer that you've just given. The word used -- the expression you say was used informally in coordination meetings, what was meant by it when it was used in this informal way? Why were the words "joint" and "command" put together in the context in which you heard them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Again, I heard the term used informally, not at any of the meetings. What this term called to mind for me was military and police structures, and military and police officials would be best placed to answer that question. Your Honour, I do wish to point out this: The meetings that I attended had no command structure to them, no command, no minutes were taken. These were working, the meetings where information was being passed along.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You've now clouded the issue further because you've already clearly said the expression was used informally but at the meetings you attended. Are you now saying it was not used in the meetings you attended but somewhere else; and if so, please tell us where?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do not remember such terms being used at any of the meetings officially, such as "Joint Command." I don't remember that kind of term being used and I definitely wish to get this clarified. I heard the term being used outside those meetings, informally, by military men, the term "Joint Command" being used. And what this implied for me was the existence of a military structure or a police structure or something like that, but that's as far as I can go in answering that question. And it really is my intention to help as much as I can. But it's quite obvious to me that your questions have to do with a hypothesis that you have on the one hand, but on the other hand, what I'm telling you is what I came across in my work and it comes down to the following sentence: There was no such thing as a Joint Command in the sense of politicians and other persons being involved, especially not in the sense of a Working Group from the SPS being involved. I hope this makes it perfectly clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: There will be a moment of silence while the Judges confer with each other.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Please continue, Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Do you recall who were the military men who used that word or that expression to you?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MATKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think I can recall any names. I'm doing my best, but I simply cannot. We would meet with representatives of the VJ in the Executive Council building and also in their own offices. It was probably then that I heard the term being used by one of them, but I can't remember who specifically or their names.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well, Mr. Matkovic. Can I move on to something else. You recall, do you, that after you were appointed by the Main Board of the party on the 10th of June, 1998, to be a part of this Working Group in respect of Kosovo, you went there with Gorica Gajevic, Mr. Andjelkovic, or Mr. Minic to get information or minutes on what the situation was in Kosovo. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MATKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do recall that meeting and the meeting that we had in Pristina. I did testify about that yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well. And subsequently on the 25th of June you returned to Belgrade and you had a meeting where you reported your findings to President Milosevic. Do you recall that meeting of the 25th of June?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MATKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And present at the meeting were the members of the Working Group, the three members of the Working Group, including yourself, Gorica Gajevic Mr. Milosevic, Mr. Milutinovic, and Mr. Sainovic. Do you remember that they were present at this meeting when you reported your findings?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MATKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I think I did say that yesterday, didn't I?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Can you recall what Mr. Milutinovic's role was at that meeting?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MATKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, when we came to the meeting we found President Milosevic there and he was the person who called that meeting, as well as Milutinovic and Sainovic. They were all already there when the four of us arrived. Three of us members of the Working Group and Ms. Gorica Gajevic was there in her capacity as secretary-general and she had been at the Pristina meeting with us, so that's why she was there. Before this we had met in her office and held a one-hour meeting and that was before we went to meet with President Milosevic --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Matkovic, please, please answer the question which is: What was Mr. Milutinovic's role at the meeting?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, Mr. Milutinovic was the president of Serbia, and I believe that he was there in that capacity. He did not take part in the discussion at that particular meeting as far as I remember; he was just there, sat in on the meeting, if that's what you're asking.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Can I take you to a later meeting. Do you recall another meeting of the 20th of June, 1998, in Belgrade, again called by Mr. Milosevic?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That's not a later meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: The 20th of July, I beg your pardon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Do you recall that meeting of the 20th of July, 1998, again convened by Mr. Milosevic in Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MATKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do remember that there was an important meeting in Belgrade with Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And I'll try to remind you some of the people who attended that meeting. Present there also was Mr. Milutinovic; Mr. Sainovic; Generals Aleksandar Dimitrijevic; Dusan Samardzic, who at the time was commander of the 3rd Army; General Perisic. Do you recall those people being there?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MATKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, now that you read out the names I do remember. You have jogged my memory.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And also there from the military side was General Pavkovic, correct? Is that correct? General Pavkovic was there?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MATKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. I remember that Pavkovic was present, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And there were also persons from the police or from the military from the Ministry of the Interior, including the minister himself, Vlajko Stojiljkovic, Vlastimir Djordjevic --

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MATKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: That is Vlastimir Djordjevic and Sreten Lukic. Do you remember them being there?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MATKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I think I do remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And -- well, before we go into the meeting can I just ask you this: Present at that meeting were members of the police, members of the army, president of the republic, president of the Federation, the deputy president of the federal government, Mr. Sainovic. So we have people from the state structures there. In what capacity were you at that meeting?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MATKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The meeting was convened by the president of the republic, and as in any other country in the world, when the president of the republic invites you, you have the honour and obligation to attend such a meeting. And I think that the president invited us as the Working Group in Kosovo, charged with dealing with the economic and political issues in Kosovo. So it was normal and natural for us to be present and to present our views from the political standpoint. But the meeting was convened by President Milosevic, and he knew the reasons why he invited all these people. The meeting was certainly of the greatest importance in your country and in any country when the president of the republic calls a meeting you know how significant it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: So it would be normal for members of the state government and the federal government to have meetings of this nature with Working Groups from the party present and participating?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MATKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't say that it was customary. This meeting was convened because of extremely important and disturbing events in Kosovo which were important not for Serbia but the whole world. I was following CNN reports, daily reports, about events in Kosovo --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I see, very well.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MATKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- so it was really an emergency situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Now, at that meeting Mr. Milutinovic -- Mr. Milosevic said that plans for an anti-terrorist programme were going to be adopted and that all of you, including your group from the party and other -- other persons from the various state bodies, had parts to play in this programme. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MATKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you see, it was an extremely important meeting and there are things that one really does remember and less important things that one forgets. So this is one of the events that I remember quite well, although it took place many years ago. And Mr. Milosevic said that the situation was serious, extremely important, and that each one should give his utmost. And he made a proposal for this plan of anti-terrorist struggle to be adopted, which would consist of several stages, and the proposal was made and elaborated upon by General Pavkovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: So General Pavkovic proposed or presented this plan, and did you all agree upon it?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MATKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was not a question of the three or four of us politicians agreeing. President Milosevic said that this plan was adopted and that this -- it had to be implemented, that it was the duty of the army. And we felt that we had to do our part of the work, meaning to ensure the functioning of the economy, to work on the political situation, et cetera. So this is implied.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Did --

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MATKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, we were not there in the capacity of people who were supposed to vote and adopt a programme. We were there to hear it, to be informed. When General Pavkovic explained these future anti-terrorist actions, Milosevic said that it should be implemented and there was not a question of us agreeing or disagreeing or voting on it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I see. Part of the plan for that meeting was an offensive or an offensive, a military and police offensive against the KLA in the summer; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MATKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think so, but I would change the terminology. It wasn't an offensive against the KLA. It was anti-terrorist activity to suppress terrorism in Kosovo, and terrorism in Kosovo took the form of the activities of the KLA. So the struggle to suppress terrorism in Kosovo, that is how I would put it. And Pavkovic elaborated on it on behalf of the army, and I assume that when he did so the commander of the 3rd Army was present and the Chief of Staff, then that he had previously along his chain of command received support for this and the same applies to the police. They coordinate their plans along their own chain of commands, and then they present it to the president of the state.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I see. Could I take you to -- before we do that there is one thing I forgot to ask you. Can you remember the role that Mr. Milutinovic played in that meeting? Did he say anything?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MATKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember Mr. Milutinovic being active at that meeting and taking part in the discussion. I really do not remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: There was another meeting convened by Mr. Milosevic that I wish to ask you about, and that is the meeting of September 10, 1998. Do you recall that meeting, it was just with Mr. Milosevic, Mr. Minic, Mr. Andjelkovic, and yourself?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MATKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, yes, yes, you've reminded me now. I do remember. And I remember roughly the purpose of that meeting. Will you ask your question or do you want me to tell you?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Please, what was the purpose of that meeting?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MATKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Unlike the meeting in July when the central issue was the struggle against terrorism, which had really taken -- had developed extensively, now the struggle against terrorism was being reduced in degree. The KLA had reduced its activity. And then this Working Group for political issues met to --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MATKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- play an increasingly important role in the functioning of state institutions and bringing life back to normal. And it was along those lines that there was the proposal to form the Temporary Executive Council. That was the purpose of that meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: So at that meeting Mr. Milosevic decided to form the Temporary Executive Council; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MATKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He accepted the proposal to form a Temporary Executive Council, and the proposal came from the political structures in Kosovo, which we had reviewed and passed on to the Executive Board and our secretary-general and the president, and the president agreed in order to help life take a normal course; that was the purpose of this Temporary Executive Council, to take care of regular supplies, production, for this academic year to get started, education, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I have nothing further for this witness, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Stamp. Mr. Fila.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise. I hadn't noted that Mr. Stamp had finished.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Matkovic, I have just a few questions for you even though you answered most of them. We were -- we mentioned the Main Board of the SPS for the Working Group to go to Kosovo, and we've discussed this at length. And we've also seen the document of the Main Board. I wish to ask you the following, please give me a yes or no answer if possible. When he nominated you to the Working Group, did President Milosevic or anyone else at that meeting use the term "Joint Command"?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MATKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: You told us that when you arrived in Kosovo you first had fewer meetings, but later they became on a daily basis with representatives of state institutions, and I'm thinking of the army now. At any of those meetings, when those meetings were quite rare, was it decided that these meetings should be referred to as the Joint Command?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MATKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I categorically assert that that was not the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: When you went to these meetings that you described as meetings for the purpose of the exchange of information, did you personally or the Working Group did give commands, issue orders, or did anyone outside the Working Group issue commands and orders to that Working Group at meetings?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MATKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The general answer is no, but it needs a lot of explaining to show that that was impossible. I was saying this yesterday and I wish to underline that it was impossible for anyone outside the structures of the police and the army to give them instructions. Because you all know better than I do that there was a hierarchy, subordination, a chain -- going from the corps to the forward command, the General Staff or the army, General Lukic, General Djordjevic, the minister of the interior. So it is absolutely not reasonable to imagine anyone outside those bodies to issue orders, not to mention a serious state faced with such a situation as we were at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: The Prosecutor, Mr. Hannis, insisted repeatedly, and you refuted those assertions, that those were meetings, the meetings that you attended, were meetings of the Joint Command and you described what took place at those meetings as you saw it. In your opinion, what should have happened at the meetings that you attended for them to be able to be referred to as a Joint Command?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: He's asking the witness to speculate. The question is vague and it invites the witness to give speculative replies.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I explain?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The point has been made so often, Mr. Stamp, that it would be futile to stop the question at this particular stage. So please proceed, Mr. Fila.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: I asked you, since you have described what was going on at those meetings, don't do that again, because it would be repetitious. What would need to happen at those meetings for it to be able to be called a command or a Joint Command?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MATKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I hope that this will be for the last time that I will be giving an explanation. After yesterday's testimony I gathered more information. For it to be a Joint Command there must be a document forming it, which doesn't exist. It needs to have a command post, a commander, reports, minutes which are adopted at every meeting, and briefings on the implementation of tasks. Not a single of these elements existed in the case of the meetings which I attended, and that was how yesterday I endeavoured to explain to Their Honours and the Prosecutor that the meetings I attended do not have the characteristics of a Joint Command and were not a Joint Command. They were consultative information meetings in a situation of extraordinary importance, not just for Serbia but for the world, at which we exchanged information.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: If anyone were to say that this was the Joint Command, would you agree or not agree with it?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MATKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If somebody used that term, then it's up to them and those people should be asked. I explained that this was not officially used and that I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: The Prosecutor showed you P1468.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So could this document be shown once again to the witness, especially the second page, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Just before you do look at that document, you said a moment ago that after yesterday's testimony you gathered more information. What did you do to gather more information?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I went home after testifying and I was explaining -- I was told that I was under oath. Of course I didn't have any communication with anyone. I sat at home and I read through the encyclopedia that my children have and that I have in my library what a command means, commanding, control and command, and a Joint Command, and this only confirmed my opinions and the truthfulness of what I told you yesterday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Fila.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: As I said, could the witness be shown, please, Exhibit P1468, page 2.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I think he has that.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Mr. Matkovic, in the third line it says "ZK" and there's a date.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MATKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't see that. Just a moment, please. Apparently this is not the same page.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Page 2, please.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MATKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ah, the second line.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: You see the date? K0228413, K0228413.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MATKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it's okay. I can see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: And you see the date of the meeting, that was the first meeting in this document, if it's a document that you have received?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MATKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my opinion, this is not an official document.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Yes, we've heard you say that. The first date mentioned is the 22nd of July, 1998. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MATKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: You have looked at this document. All the subsequent meetings were held later. My question is: Before the 22nd of July, did you hold meetings with the people listed here individually or all of them together? You see there are representatives of the army and the police. Did you have any meetings of that kind earlier on?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MATKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, we had meetings linked to the Belacevac open-cast mine when the terrorists broke in and abducted the workers, and then we went to see General Djordjevic and General Pavkovic and we asked them for their assistance because that was what the people demanded of us.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: My question -- my next question is: The meetings that preceded this one on the 22nd of July, were they referred to as a Joint Command or did you decide at any of those meetings that the meetings that would be held after the 22nd of July would be called "Joint Command"?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MATKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: If I understood you correctly, the previous meetings do not differ from these meetings after the 22nd of July, do they?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MATKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not in essence. All these meetings were devoted to information and coordination of activities to bring life back to normal.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: The Prosecutor showed you the minutes from a meeting held on the 29th of October. You answered that question. Thank you, Mr. Matkovic, you already answered more than half the questions I had intended to ask you and thank you for your kindness and for coming to testify.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have no further questions for this witness, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Fila.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Matkovic, how were the meetings that are recorded in that document convened?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MATKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean the last document that Mr. Fila has showed me, the meeting of the ZK for KiM?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes, how were you notified of these meetings?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MATKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, I will take the liberty of reminding you that I talked about this yesterday but I will repeat. Following the meeting on the 20th of July, the meeting held in President Milosevic's office when the situation was very difficult, we all realised that the situation was exceptionally serious and that we had to work at full tilt, each in our own respective jobs. So we travelled to Pristina. And, quite simply, the need arose because there was a lot of information coming in every day about roads being blocked about houses being attacked about rapes and murder about factories being put out of operation. We all had to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Matkovic, Mr. Matkovic, just --

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MATKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm about to wrap it up, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, what you've told us so far is useless, so please tell us something that answers the question.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MATKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I was just about to say that there was a need for communication, for exchanging information, and we agreed to meet in the Executive Council building at the time of the evening news, the Serbian TV evening news, so we could watch the evening news all together and exchange information. That's how this initiative first came about and that's when it started happening, and it soon grew to be on a daily basis or at least it was from time to time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Before it became daily, though, how did you know which days to meet together?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MATKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, many serious incidents were happening every day and we spoke to each other on the phone, and we probably told each other at the time, Let's all get together, let's all see what we can do. I remember with particular vividness what happened in Orahovac when that 50 or even a hundred people from Orahovac simply went straight into the building, and we had to call someone from the army or from the police to see what we could do about this because citizens required action. An Albanian was killed because he wouldn't allow his daughter or son to be recruited into the Kosovo Liberation Army. They killed him in a grewsome way so the local Albanians called us over and, of course, we passed the message over to General Djordjevic, to General Pavkovic that we should meet. We phoned them, we started meeting, and over time - and I think you understand this situation full well - this became an exchange of information for which there was a real need.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Who was it that informed you of the time and the place that you should meet when you were not meeting on a daily basis? Who was the person who took these decisions?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MATKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't call those decisions. There was a need for communicating, for holding meetings. Very often the initiative meetings would come from the three of us and we were all sitting in the same offices. I said yesterday to call people, to get together, to exchange information. Every day we were in contact with the citizens, with the people there, and they were facing a great amount of hardship. We were under a lot of pressure to provide some answers as to what would become of the Belacevac mine, the abductees of the Orahovac -- why was this factory now out of operation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We do not need to hear all these events again. We just are trying to understand how this group of people just happened according to you to come together without anyone identifying where you would meet and when. Now, can you help us with that? There must have been somebody who ultimately decided that it was necessary to meet and the time that it was necessary to meet.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MATKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, I understand your need to make this communication come across as something that was actually under some sort of command or something that was organised, but believe me - and I'm telling you this under oath - those were spontaneous meetings in keeping with our real needs at the time and the difficult situation that prevailed in Kosovo at the time. There were daily phone calls five or ten times a day because of all the problems that we were facing. It's very difficult to single out now a single call to pin-point a single call saying we should meet at this time or that time. But it became our established practice to meet at 7.30 in the evening, during the evening news. That was when we met because the situation was quite exceptional. People were being killed, people were being sniped at. Please, believe me, this wasn't it something that was organised. The situation in Kosovo was dramatic. We met in order to try to find a way to help each other. I am really doing my best to help the Tribunal and I am saying the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Stamp, anything you want to ask arising out of that?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: No questions, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Fila?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Matkovic, that completes your evidence here; thank you for coming to give it. You're now free to leave the room where you're sitting.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, too, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Fila, who is the next witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, Zoran Andjelkovic is our next witness, and I think he's about to be shown into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Two things I can deal with while that's happening. Because of the changed arrangements this afternoon, we'll sit until 4.00 and then break for 20 minutes. And we'll sit then for an hour until 5.40 and have another 20-minute break. So that will become two one-hour sessions following this one. The other matter is this: You have invited us to admit documents from the bar table. A preliminary consideration of that application indicates that quite a number of them, probably just over 50, have already been admitted and we will identify these and make the position clear, but there are a number of others where there is an absence of any real indication of their reliability. We would invite you to make a supplementary filing providing such further information as you can about the source of these documents and any features indicating reliability and anything else you can think of. And I'm going to give you a list of these now. They're all documents which are just on plain paper with no headings, signatures, or seals, they are as follows: 2D - and I won't repeat 2D - 63, 204, 265, 268, 280, 281, 285, 287, 288, 289, 295, 300, and 304. If it was possible for you to do that for tomorrow, it would be helpful; but we understand the load that you're carrying at this moment. Mr. Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, if I may. We'll try to deal with this as quickly as possible. May the deadline be set for next Monday. I hope that's acceptable to the Chamber. At first sight - and we shall be submitting this in writing - when looking at these documents, these documents were obtained through the national committee for cooperation with The Hague Tribunal and they were obtained from appropriate archives. Specifically, I think these documents are announcements from meetings of the federal government and the archives of the federal government is where those documents came from, but I won't waste any of the Chamber's time now. We shall be filing our written submissions in order to explain how and from which source each of these documents were obtained.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Let me give you just an example of the sort of problem that we're facing. Some of them are drafts and they bear to be the conclusions of the National Assembly, but on the -- on further reading they could, in fact, be proposals from a party and perhaps they ultimately became the conclusions of the National Assembly. But there are certain weaknesses about the form of these documents that cause us to seek a little more clarification about their exact role, and therefore their authenticity as what you claim them to be. So if you could give attention to that, it would be of assistance. We're obviously anxious to admit from the bar table all that you wish us to admit that's relevant to your case, particularly where there's no objection to this taken by the Prosecution. But there are limits to how much leeway there can be about documents that -- about which questions might be asked. So please do what you can to assist.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, we shall do just that, and I hope that we'll succeed in convincing you that the documents should qualify for admission by the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Andjelkovic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Would you please make the solemn declaration to speak the truth by reading aloud the document which will now be placed before you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Please be seated. Mr. Andjelkovic, you will now be examined by Mr. Fila on behalf of Mr. Sainovic. Mr. Fila.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN ANDJELKOVIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: First of all, state your name, please. Tell us which state and party positions you held back in 1998 and 1999, but please one step at a time. First I finish my question then there's the interpretation and then you go.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN ANDJELKOVIC
utterances.text: My name is Zoran Andjelkovic. Back in 1998 and 1999 I was a member of the Main Board of the party. As for my state position, as for the 24th of March, 1998, I was minister for youth and sport. As of the 28th of September, 1998, I was president of the Temporary Executive Council. I was also in charge of a working body in Serbia's [Realtime transcript read in error: "body"] government.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Which one?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN ANDJELKOVIC
utterances.text: The personnel commission.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: At one point in time --

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My apologies. It should be in Serbia's government and not in Serbia's body.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: At one point in time you left for Kosovo; can you explain why?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN ANDJELKOVIC
utterances.text: I went to Kosovo following a decision of the Main Board of the Socialist Party of Serbia at a meeting that was held on the 10th of June, 1998. The Main Board then numbered over 300 members, as it does now. In most cases, presidents of municipal organisations are called so that amounts to over 400 people. The Main Board reviewed the situation, the overall situation, throughout Serbia. Mr. Mirko Marjanovic, the prime minister contributed something about the economic situation; Ms. Gajevic spoke about the activities undertaken by the socialist party; and Mr. Minic spoke about the political problems and security problems in Kosovo and Metohija. At the close of that session the conclusion was reached that a Working Group should be set up to be headed by Mr. Minic. Mr. Matkovic, vice-president of the Main Board, and I as a member of the Main Board were members of that Working Group.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: At the time, did the state bodies of Serbia and Yugoslavia start strengthening their presence in Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN ANDJELKOVIC
utterances.text: Indeed. That was, after all, one of the conclusions reached by the Main Board. Both state and party bodies were to dispatch their people down to Kosovo so that they might help stabilise the political situation. I know that for sometime in the preceding period the republican government, the Government of the Republic of Serbia, picked a coordinator for the work of the state bodies in Kosovo and Metohija, and this was Minister Andreja Milosavljevic. The federal government in its term had nominated Mr. Nikola Sainovic. The Ministry of Foreign Affairs set up a headquarters in Pristina, and other ministries, too, had the responsibility of sending their own assistants down to Kosovo and Metohija to help along.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Why, in your opinion, did the federal government dispatch Nikola Sainovic of all people to Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN ANDJELKOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Sainovic was deputy prime minister and he was in charge of foreign policy. Everyone in Serbia knew that the situation in Kosovo and Metohija security-wise and in political terms would soon be internationalised in the sense of a growing presence of international players, international agents in Kosovo and Metohija.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: So your group of three arrived in Kosovo. What did you find when you got there?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN ANDJELKOVIC
utterances.text: I must say that before this I had been to Kosovo twice. I was there for the signing of the education agreement, which was signed by Mr. Agani, and I was there to talk to the dean and rectors of the Pristina University. These were talks surrounding the conclusion of that agreement, and then sometime late in June we were off as the Working Group I think on or about the 25th. We went there to attend a meeting of the provincial board. The situation was extremely serious. All the main roads, all the principal roads, in Kosovo and Metohija were blocked. Several dozens of people had been kidnapped by this time. Belacevac, which is an open-cast mine, which provides -- which provides energy for some other factories, was blocked and many of the Serb villages were under permanent attacks.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: So your group of three, when you arrived there, what did each of you do, briefly, please?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN ANDJELKOVIC
utterances.text: We were located in the provincial board. Mr. Minic was in charge of political talks with the provincial leaders. Mr. Matkovic was -- happened to be the manager of Sartid was touring Kosovo's companies, trying to keep production up and running and to kick-start production in some places in factories that had ceased to operate. I toured various areas in Kosovo and Metohija in a bid to talk to everyone there and in a bid to convince them not to leave their areas in order to prevent an exodus. I worked with Mr. Milosavljevic on humanitarian issues, and we were doing everything in our power to bring the internally displaced back to their homes to help them re-build their homes. I was also constantly working on the agreement and the implementation of the agreement.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: What about Mr. Sainovic, he was there on behalf of the federal government --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honours, page 30, line 2, the witness said that he was working on the education agreement and the implementation of the education agreement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Zecevic. Mr. Fila.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Mr. Sainovic was there on behalf of the federal government, as you said. Was he subordinated to you? Was he your superior in any way, I mean subordinated or superior to the group of three.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN ANDJELKOVIC
utterances.text: Neither subordinated nor superior nor was Andreja Milosavljevic in his capacity as minister nor were all the assistant ministers who were there subordinated or superior to us; we were all doing our jobs.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Throughout the time you spent in Kosovo as a member of the Working Group, were meetings held of various state bodies working in Kosovo and Metohija, meetings that the Working Group attended, that all of its three members attended?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN ANDJELKOVIC
utterances.text: Our political activity consisted of holding meetings. Needless to say, we would meet mayors, municipality presidents, representatives of state bodies, but those were meetings where information was exchanged because without exchanging information, while one couldn't just go to a specific area, for example, see the citizens of Belacevac and promise them that the state would do something about the kidnapping that the state would in due course be taking certain measures, just by way of an example.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: How often did you have these meetings?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN ANDJELKOVIC
utterances.text: Depends on which particular meetings you have in mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: With the state bodies, with the police and the military present. ?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN ANDJELKOVIC
utterances.text: Oh, the state bodies, the military and the police, well, in late July, August, and September we held meetings quite often and there were several meetings in October, too.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: What about before then?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN ANDJELKOVIC
utterances.text: We met several times or saw each other several times or spoke to each other several times.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: All right. Those meetings beginning in late July and going on throughout August and September, as you claim, did you hear anyone refer to those meetings as meetings of the Joint Command for Kosovo and Metohija?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN ANDJELKOVIC
utterances.text: I do have to be completely sincere because I took an oath. I never heard of these meetings being described as meetings of some sort of Joint Command. The first time I laid eyes on any reference like that was when I spoke to Mr. Curtis on the 8th of February, 2004. During that interview I heard various terms being used while I was in Kosovo and Metohija, staff, joint staff, corps command, IKM, 3A IKM, PRK Djakovica, but these were terms that meant nothing to me. For example, in late September and October I heard a term ZK for KiM being used, but these terms meant nothing to me but I wasn't exactly wondering at the time. I didn't believe that this had anything to do with us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Page 31, line 24, the witness said in "September," whereas the transcript reflects November.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Fila, I don't speak English but I suppose there's another error here. I said IKM 3A then followed by a comma and then IKM --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Could the witness and counsel please be asked to not speak at the same time. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You've got that message, Mr. Fila, have you, that there's a cross-over between you and that's resulted in us not getting the clarification that the witness sought to give. Please say that again, Mr. Andjelkovic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Your Honour. I don't speak English myself, but of course it's easy to see these abbreviations, isn't it. It's right there. It's coming off the screen now. It's IKM, 3A IKM, and then a comma and then IKM Berka Djakovica. Not Berka, Prka, P-r-k-a -- P-r-k.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Can we continue with these meetings. Were the same persons always present at these meetings or --

utterances.speaker: ZORAN ANDJELKOVIC
utterances.text: No, my apologies. No, not the same persons. There were always those who were absent that were present and some people came over from Belgrade, they liked taking their coffee at 7.30 in the evening so the persons present at those meeting were almost never the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Why, when, and by whose decision was the Temporary Executive Council in Kosovo set up and what were your responsibilities?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN ANDJELKOVIC
utterances.text: The Temporary Executive Council was set up by a decision of Serbia's Assembly on the 28th of September, 1998. Serbia's Assembly, as item number 1 on its agenda, adopted a report on the events in Kosovo and Metohija and appropriate conclusions. Item 2 on the agenda comprised a decision to set up a Temporary Executive Council. Item 3 contained a decision to appoint a minister of Serbia's government as president of the Temporary Executive Council, Zoran Andjelkovic. And then item 4 was he was within a seven-day period to appoint members to that body. The Temporary Executive Council, first and foremost, had the following tasks: Firstly, to show Serbia's good-will to reach a political agreement as soon as possible, to have an election as soon as possible, and to constitute appropriate authorities, an Assembly, and some sort of Executive Council, therefore. As for the jurisdiction of the Executive Council, this would be detailed in the agreement and it would henceforth have the jurisdiction agreed upon in that agreement. For this reason this Executive Council, above all, had a social and humanitarian aspect.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [No interpretation].

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters didn't hear the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Could you repeat that question.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Did you appoint members to the Temporary Executive Council?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN ANDJELKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. On the 3rd of October, a week later, I appointed at the first founding meeting members of the Temporary Executive Council. There were a total of 16, five of them Serbs and 11 of them non-Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: My last question before the break, sir, did Nikola Sainovic have anything to do with the Temporary Executive Council?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN ANDJELKOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I've just looked at the clock. This might be the right time for our break, and I've just finished with this particular subject.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Fila. Mr. Andjelkovic, we need to have a break at this stage, that will be for 20 minutes. Could you please leave the courtroom with the usher.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And we shall resume at 4.20.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Fila.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Let us now move on to another topic, Mr. Andjelkovic. The term "local security" has been mentioned here, so we would like to hear from you what that means.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN ANDJELKOVIC
utterances.text: Local security is an attempt through this particular activity to restore the confidence of the Albanian national community and to ensure in the first stage in Albanian villages that individuals and groups in communication with the leadership of the municipality and its local parties of self-government would be responsible for humanitarian issues, for humanitarian aid, for supplies for the population with humanitarian aid, and organised supplies and distribution that was on a commercial basis and also through the republic headquarters for the supply of basic foodstuffs, which were running short. Their task also was to thereby ensure conditions in which there would be no need for the state police to enter such Albanian villages unless there were any serious conflicts.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: You mentioned Albanian villages. Was this envisaged just for Albanian villages?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN ANDJELKOVIC
utterances.text: No. This was one stage, or rather, the first step, but the next step would be in all settlements and villages in mixed villages. There was a major effort for the village of Kijevo, which was inhabited by both Albanians, Romanis, and Serbs, and we endeavoured through political means to set up such a local security in that village. And we discussed this with the local leadership of the municipality of Klina. Unfortunately ...

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Was there resistance to the formation of such local security; and if so, from where did it come?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN ANDJELKOVIC
utterances.text: Unfortunately, yes, and there was a great deal of resistance in fact, and this is obvious since this activity did not succeed, both by Albanian extremists and Serb nationalists; obviously they shared a common goal.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: And when did you give up those efforts?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN ANDJELKOVIC
utterances.text: We worked on it politically for as long as we were there, but in actual fact, by October already there was -- it was evident that nothing would come of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Did Mr. Sainovic have anything to do with local security in any sense?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN ANDJELKOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Sainovic did not. This was up to the municipalities, the presidents of municipalities, and the local government. Politically he supported it, as we did from the Working Group, as well as the other people who were there and who wanted to achieve some sort of rapprochement among the ethnic communities.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Mentioning Mr. Sainovic, do you know what his work was in Kosovo and Metohija in 1998?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN ANDJELKOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Sainovic was the deputy prime minister in charge of international cooperation, and I think that up until the arrival of the OSCE delegation he had dozens of meetings with Mr. Hill, I think, and we -- when we contacted representatives of the international community we would always consult Mr. Sainovic. And after the OSCE mission came to Kosovo then the organisation was changed, or rather, we acquired different roles. Ten days prior to that I had become president of the Temporary Executive Council, the federal government had formed a commission for cooperation with the OSCE, which consisted of representatives of both republican and federal bodies, and he continued working in that area so that we had less occasion to act in that field.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: And what position did he hold?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN ANDJELKOVIC
utterances.text: He was president of the commission for cooperation with the OSCE on behalf of the -- it was a commission of the federal government.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: As you became the president of the Temporary Executive Council and acted as such in Kosovo from then on, what was the position of the government of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia and the Republic of Serbia towards the OSCE mission?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN ANDJELKOVIC
utterances.text: I'm deeply convinced that the position and aim of all competent state bodies, and especially those of us who were down there in Kosovo, that this was a good idea, that this was asserting the policy of Serbia and Yugoslavia and that it was useful for dealing with the problems in Kosovo and Metohija and that this would speed up the finding of a final political solution in Kosovo and Metohija. The first contact I had with representatives of the OSCE resulted in the decision that we should make a population census and organise elections within a period of nine months and set up bodies, because the expectation was that in those nine months a political settlement would be achieved and on that basis organs set up and especially on the basis of the Milosevic-Holbrooke Agreement.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Do you know how it came about that Nikola Sainovic was included in our delegation for the negotiations in Rambouillet?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN ANDJELKOVIC
utterances.text: One evening Ms. Gajevic, the secretary of our party, called me up and said that the delegation for Rambouillet should consist also of representatives of ethnic communities who were members of the Temporary Executive Council. I saw the composition of that delegation and I thought that it should be strengthened. I proposed several names, including the president of the republic, Mr. Milosevic, and Mr. Sainovic, in view of the fact that he was the vice-president for international cooperation. And it seemed logical to me that Mr. Hill would be in Rambouillet, with whom Mr. Sainovic had had several talks.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know anything about Nikola Sainovic's activities after the war broke out, I mean activities in Kosovo and Metohija?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN ANDJELKOVIC
utterances.text: I saw Mr. Sainovic after the war started several times in Kosovo. On the 28th of March we saw each other at the opening of the reconstructed student hostel at Pristina University and in April I saw him several times. He came to see me before or after his talks with Mr. Rugova, and I know that on one occasion he asked me for the Executive Council to assist in humanitarian terms Rugova's family. I think there were 34 people in the house that Boris [as interpreted] Rugova was living in, and I assigned the secretary of the Temporary Executive Council to provide everything ranging from pampers, diapers, flour, sugar, and everything else to be taken to Mr. Rugova's home.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Are you aware of Sainovic's visit to Pristina in the beginning of July 1999?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN ANDJELKOVIC
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, that was when the talks had already started between Ahtissari and Milosevic and I know that Mr. Sainovic did come to Pristina.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... what is intended, I'm not sure, on line 14.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, we'll find out. Please continue for the moment, Mr. Fila.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could I make a correction. I'm talking about June 1999. I asked about June, not July.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Do you know anything about this Joint Command that I asked you about relating to 1998? Do you know whether there was a Joint Command for Kosovo during the war in 1999, of which you were a member and Nikola Sainovic the commander?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN ANDJELKOVIC
utterances.text: Quite certainly I guarantee that this was not possible to have such a body with civilians in it. I saw representatives of the army for the last time before the beginning of the bombing and towards the end, when the Milosevic-Holbrooke Agreement was about to be signed. They left Pristina, so we couldn't see each other or hear each other. So when you asked me whether there were commands, I really don't know. But any command of which civilians were a part - and that means myself and Nikola Sainovic - certainly not.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Do you remember attending a meeting held on the 1st of June, 1999, in the cellar, in the basement, of the Grand Hotel?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN ANDJELKOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Sainovic, probably it was on the 1st of June but around that time, came to see me in the Executive Council. We had a cup of coffee, and like any good host I offered to host lunch or dinner because it was quite late, and Mr. Sainovic said that we had been invited to the Grand Hotel at -- by representatives of the army and that they would host a dinner. So we went to this basement, which is about two levels below the lobby level. Sometimes I think not billiards -- bowling, there was a bowling alley there. In the middle of the table there was some PCs. I gather that this was an information centre because that was logical that this was the media centre for communication with the press. I think that General Vasiljevic was present and some other generals whom I don't know probably from the Supreme Command or from the 3rd Army, whatever they're called. And each of the persons presented what they knew about what was going on in the field. Mr. Sainovic spoke about the talks in Belgrade between Ahtissari, Chernomyrdin and Milosevic. Representatives of the army spoke of attacks on the border with Albania and the daily raids that were taking place centimetre by centimetre in that area, and we had dinner there.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Andjelkovic, was this a meeting of the Joint Command? Did anyone report to Sainovic or brief him? Did Sainovic issue any orders, instructions, or the like at that meeting?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN ANDJELKOVIC
utterances.text: This was an exchange of information meeting for -- those of us who were in Pristina on a longer basis, we wanted to know how the talks and negotiations in Belgrade were developing and when this would end, and of course Mr. Sainovic was interested as to what was going on on the ground. Therefore, there was no briefing of anyone or reporting to anyone, but there was an exchange of information. This under any circumstances could not have been a command, a Joint Command. We just came there.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: In line 17 the word "as guests" was left out, we just came there as guests.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Fila.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: We heard from a witness when you and Mr. Sainovic entered, those who were sitting down there got up. Is that strange? Is it strange when the vice-president of the federal government walks in for the other people to get up?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN ANDJELKOVIC
utterances.text: I really didn't understand your question. I think this is customary. When somebody comes to visit you at home, even when he is not the vice-premier, when somebody comes to your office, it's only logical for you to get up and greet him even if he doesn't have any high-ranking position, it is a normal good custom in Serbia, and if people didn't stand up, that would be considered quite shameful. It would mean that the person was not welcome.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: According to our customs, would it be insulting for people to keep their sheets?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN ANDJELKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I said ashamed, shame, and insulting is more or less the same. This is simply customary. I was vice-president of the Assembly, and even when the president of the municipality comes to see you, you get up, even when he's of a lower rank than you are. This is quite normal.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Just in one sentence, as you spent a certain amount of time in Kosovo with Sainovic as of 1998, would you tell us what his positions were regarding a settlement for Kosovo and Metohija, what kind of a person he was?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN ANDJELKOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Sainovic is an extremely hard-working man. He can work for 15 hours a day. He comes from a mining environment, and they are mostly multi-ethnic and he knows what it means to live in a multi-ethnic environment. And whenever I spoke to him he was sincere in seeking to achieve peace and tolerance in Kosovo and Metohija. This is something I'm quite certain of, and he was always worried and concerned and disturbed about anything -- any reports that were negative about developments in Kosovo and Metohija --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could there be a pause, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Fila, you're not pausing between the answer and your question. Can you start that question again.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My last question.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Mr. Andjelkovic, did representatives of the Tribunal come to see you; and if they did, why and when and what did you do?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN ANDJELKOVIC
utterances.text: I had two encounters with representatives of the Tribunal; one was in November 2003, it was very brief, 10 or 15 minutes only, because I asked them to have this meeting in 2004 because there was a party congress being prepared, the Socialist Party of Serbia, and to be quite sincere, we were working on certain reforms. And as president of the Main Board, I was ready to talk to them but I asked them if we could have this interview in 2004. Mr. Curtis and Ms. Marina and another lady came to see me, and we talked on the 7th and 8th of February, 2004. We agreed on several points at the very beginning; one is that I wanted to help in establishing the truth here in The Hague Tribunal and that is why I wanted to talk to them. At their request to be a witness of the Prosecution against Slobodan Milosevic. I said I really couldn't do that because I was the secretary-general of the Socialist Party of Serbia, of which Milosevic was still nominally the president. That if the Trial Chamber decided I would be ready to come, that this was simply an interview but I did not wish to make a statement because it could be used in the political campaign against me. Unfortunately, on the 8th, on Sunday, we spoke outside of town and the national television carried a report on my conversation with representatives of The Hague Tribunal. As a result, I and my family had hundreds of telephone calls and threats, and on the 10th I didn't dare look at the text of the notes she had made. I saw those notes for the first time when I came to The Hague in English. Unfortunately I don't speak English. This is a major shortcoming of mine, but what can I do? The site translation I received, as in any notes done in this way, there's a lack of precision and some factual errors. Let me give you an example, just one. It says that I was president of the youth of Yugoslavia in 1988, but that's not the problem. The president was Hashim Rexhepi, a great friend of mine, a Kosovo Albanian, and if he were to see this he would think that I wanted to insult him and that is the least thing I had on my mind. There was, anyway, a lot of imprecision and factual errors.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That would be all, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: When was it that you saw the notes in English?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Two or three days ago when I arrived in The Hague. Your Honour, I was never called by anyone nor were the notes served on me, and my thought was: Why didn't we do that on the 10th of February.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Were you listed as a witness for the Defence in the Milosevic trial?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. I was not listed as a Defence witness for Mr. Milosevic, and that was why a campaign was launched against me by certain members of the Socialist Party.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Any Defence counsel wish to cross-examine?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, if I may, I said at the time that I did not wish to be an OTP witness or a Defence witness, but should the Chamber rule on the matter they should simply call my number and I would be there. That is exactly what I told The Hague Prosecutors at the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Bakrac.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I hope that I'll be very brief.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Mr. Andjelkovic, I'm Mihajlo Bakrac and I'm here on behalf of General Lazarevic.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN ANDJELKOVIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: I'll ask you two or three questions briefly. First of all, I do have to ask you this. Can you please look at an exhibit presented by a Defence team, it's about to come up on the screen in front of you. This is an e-court exhibit 5D412.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can that please be brought up on our screens. If we could please zoom in slightly.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Mr. Andjelkovic, and I'll be asking you now -- first of all, can you see the document?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN ANDJELKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I can, I've just put on my glasses.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Please have a look. It's not a long document. Read it for yourself and then I'll be asking you two or three questions about it. Have you read it, sir?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN ANDJELKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: First of all, do you recognise this document?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN ANDJELKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Markovic showed me this document; he was in charge of that particular sector in the Executive Council.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: When you say that Mr. Markovic showed you this document and he was in charge of that sector, would I be right in stating that this was shown to you in May 1999?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN ANDJELKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, of course, we did speak about that, didn't we, and we took certain measures. I know for a fact -- may I continue?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Well, just to be as quick as possible, I'll ask you questions and I think that that might hurry us along a little. This is information from the commander of the Pristina Corps, General Vladimir Lazarevic, and he requests here that the Temporary Executive Council take urgent action in the town of Glogovac to feed the population, provide health care for the population. Is that true, sir?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN ANDJELKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Following this letter, did you as the Temporary Executive Council do anything about that?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN ANDJELKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, and not just in this particular town. There are video records and clips showing that. We were involved in providing humanitarian aid to the population, specifically in Glogovac the Working Group was headed by Mr. Faik Jashari, the Working Group delivering humanitarian aid to the town. I think he was with Ms. Abderisa, with Vule Andric and some other people and they personally delivered it. I saw the tape about villages around Glogovac to which they delivered humanitarian aid and I saw them carry medical supplies, too. This is pursuant to an agreement that we had to take measures to do whatever could. However, Mr. Bakrac, I do have to say, that throughout the war we had a huge shortage of foodstuffs and humanitarian aid supplies and this is something that we always underlined.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Mr. Andjelkovic, thank you. I have just another question for you. Be so kind, please, as far as I know you were familiar with the situation in Kosovo and were at the time. The town of Glogovac, what is the ethnic make-up of the town of Glogovac?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN ANDJELKOVIC
utterances.text: As far as I remember, there were one or two Serb families. Everybody else was Albanian.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
