utterances.text: You will agree with me, therefore, that the aid was requested and received by the Albanian population?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN ANDJELKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, of course. Most of the aid during the NATO air-strikes provided by the Temporary Executive Council and our commission for humanitarian aid was meant for the Albanian population.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Andjelkovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour, I do have a few questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Andjelkovic, my name is Dan Ivetic and I am the attorney for Sreten Lukic.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN ANDJELKOVIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I have a few questions for you to clarify some things so I beg your indulgence. First of all, in conducting your duties at the Temporary Executive Council for Kosovo and Metohija, do you recall any instances in 1998 where you interacted with foreign diplomats of any NATO countries such as my own, the United States of America, wherein the diplomats personally expressed to you their attitude or reaction towards the killings, kidnappings, and other terrorist acts undertaken by the KLA?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN ANDJELKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, in actual fact, from October to the very end of 1998, I had the best part of those talks until the beginning of the NATO air-strikes. I think the 20th -- on the 21st of March, 1999, there was a meeting with Mr. Vollebaek. As for 1998, yes, of course, I shared whatever information I had about the number of those killed and those kidnapped, about which roads were blocked and where. The Pristina-Pec road, specifically the Pec-Kosovska Mitrovica road, the Prizren road through Stimlje, Pristina itself. There was this one talk that I had, as you suggested, with representatives of the US. There was a lady - and I can't remember her name - she is a lady from the US congress. I'm sure that there is a note about that meeting in the archives of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs, because representatives of that ministry were always there for each and every one of the talks that I held. They would report back on any of my meetings. They spied on me in a manner of speaking as people say where I come from and they would write it all up. I think her name was Ms. Rosenberg she was from the US congress. I put forward my position. So many people had been killed, so many terror acts had been committed, so many people had been kidnapped. We were still unaware of the fate of so many people, and she said, "Mr. Andjelkovic, your information is probably accurate," and I said "Well, this is the information I got, I can't tell." And she said, "Now, I don't doubt the authenticity of your information but I do wish to tell you one thing. You view the Kosovo Liberation Army as a terrorist organisation; my country believes that they are freedom fighters. And we have every sympathy for freedom fighters anywhere." I told Mr. Sainovic about this once when we talked and I think he spoke to Mr. Ivanovic [as interpreted], and I think later as a result a protest note was sent to the US embassy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, page 48, line 9, this is Mr. Jovanovic, not Mr. Ivanovic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Zivadin Jovanovic, the minister of foreign affairs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, sir, I'm just waiting for the transcript to catch up with us. Now, if we can turn to the period of the NATO bombing campaign in 1999 which you mentioned, and I believe that you were in Pristina much of this time. Do you recall the bombing of the MUP building in Pristina where the Pristina SUP and the MUP staff were based and what date that occurred on?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN ANDJELKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. During the war I would spend one, two, or three days a week in Pristina. One shouldn't forget the fact that I was at the same time the federal [as interpreted] minister for youth and sport. On the day when the MUP building was bombed -- I remember that day very clearly. This was the 28th of March, if I remember, that was when we opened the student hostel. Secondly, I remember this because my window, my hotel window, affords a view of the MUP building, the distance being no more than 1 or 200 metres and I saw this happen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, if I may, page 49, line 1, it reads he was federal minister, but he wasn't and he didn't say that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was the republican minister for youth and sport.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And, sir, were you physically present to see the aftermath of the NATO attack on the MUP building?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN ANDJELKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. There was a man named Goran at the hotel. We walked over to the MUP building, not because of the building itself but it was our impression that the health station which was just next to the MUP building had been struck, too. It did catch fire because the building adjacent to it, the MUP building, had been targeted. We arrived there and we realised that the fire brigade men were trying to put out the fire in the MUP building fire was ablaze. I thought this was an insane thing to do, but there is a corridor between the buildings leading to another building that is part of a residential block and I tried to convince them to smash the window-panes along that corridor and throw the water inside to keep the fire from spreading to the adjacent building. I failed, obviously, I thought that I knew best, but we all think just that sometimes whereas those in charge of a certain job are best placed to know. So this man named Goran and I walked over to that other building across the way. Mr. Stojanovic [as interpreted] appeared. He asked me where I was headed and I told him what I was trying to do and then he came with me and Stevanovic and then we used the fire extinguishers to push the fire back in this corridor and then we smashed the glass panes. We managed to stop the fire from spreading. We saw a janitor there and Goran Stojanovic [as interpreted] when -- as we passed him said this man doesn't even know what is going on. He was an Albanian, not that it counts. On our way back we asked him what happened here and he said, well, something was just smashed and the problem being behind that building --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, if there is some detail you require, can you direct the witness to it so that we can --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: The efforts to stop the spread is what I wanted. I'm trying to actually correct the transcript, if I may. Page 50, line 6, first of all it says Mr. Stojanovic appeared; I believe the witness said Mr. Stevanovic appeared. And then later on at line 10 of the same page we saw a janitor there and Goran Stojanovic. Goran Stojanovic; I think the witness said General Stevanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And just to clarify, we're talking about General Obrad Stevanovic; is that correct, sir?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN ANDJELKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now -- now, if we can move to another event that occurred around the same time, the NATO bombing of the PTT, the telephone, telegraph and post building in Pristina. Can you describe any personal knowledge that you have of that event as, for instance, when did it occur and any observations that you made of that occurrence?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN ANDJELKOVIC
utterances.text: If I'm not mistaken I think this was on the 7th of April. I was in an office in the Temporary Executive Council when the strike occurred. The refinery first, or rather, a petrol storage facility owned by INA, which is about 7 or 8 kilometres out of Pristina. I called --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I'm trying to shorten it. I'd like to keep you here as short as possible. I'd like to direct your attention specifically to the PTT building. Were you present physically at the scene for the aftermath of that -- of that strike by the NATO bombs?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN ANDJELKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I was just trying to say that. First we went to Devet Jugovica and then Pristina was bombed and then Mr. Markovic and I drove back to the centre of Pristina and we spent the whole night trying to rescue those people, specifically a Turkish family, we rescued an elderly lady and two children; the rest of them didn't make it, unfortunately. Mr. Andric's mother-in-law came to grieve. He was a member of the Temporary Executive Council on 27th of March he was at a check-point with General Jankovic trying to provide security for the people passing through and trying to convince them to go back to Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And you mentioned the efforts to try and rescue those people. Am I correct among the casualties, in addition to the Turkish family you talked of, they were other ethnic Albanians that were the casualties of this NATO attack?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN ANDJELKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, was it a Turkish family, an Albanian family, some say Turkish, some say Albanian. Mr. Salin Goxhufi [phoen], for example, a member of the Executive Council, believed them to be Albanians but that didn't matter because there were a great number of casualties, Serbs, Albanians, and Turks in that particular street because this is the old town of Pristina, the old core of Pristina town. There were Serbs living there, Albanians, Turks, and they had been there for ages.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: There's an answer there that's not very clear, Mr. Ivetic. Mr. -- It's at line 19, Mr. Andric's mother-in-law came to grieve. He was a member of the Temporary Executive Council on 27th March.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What is this about?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I believe the witness said that she perished in the attack, but we can ask him to clarify it since I did not catch this earlier.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Where does the check-point fit in? Perhaps you can assist.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, could you please, since the transcript did not accurately reflect your answer, could you please tell us again what happened to your colleague Mr. Andric's mother-in-law and where he was at the time of the NATO strike on the PTT building in Pristina.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN ANDJELKOVIC
utterances.text: On the 27th or the 28th, as president of the Executive Council I had set up a Working Group headed by Mr. Andric, the secretary for health in the province, Professor Moracic, president of the Red Cross of Kosovo and Metohija was involved, too, and a number of other people and then on 27 and 28th they were at the Djeneral Jankovic check-point trying to help the people who were there and convince them to return. His mother-in-law came to grieve that evening right there. I'm not sure if that's essential.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Just to be clear, though, she came to grieve at the Djeneral Jankovic check-point?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sorry?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Did she come to grieve at the Djeneral --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no. In the air-strike, the centre of Pristina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Let's move on, Mr. --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] While he was at the Djeneral Jankovic check-point.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: We're waiting for the transcript again. Thank you. Now, during the time-period following these two bombings by NATO in the centre of Pristina, what were your personal observations of the effects these two bombings had on the civilian population of Pristina of all ethnicities?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN ANDJELKOVIC
utterances.text: I would say the same thing as any citizen of Pristina. Destruction, chaos, a large number of people feeling unsafe, fear, departures. Unfortunately, this is the usual consequence of any sort of destruction on that scale and that sort of panic spreading.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... the NATO bombing Pristina was hit just about every night in some form or another by NATO armaments?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN ANDJELKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, to the extent that I could see, Pristina and its surroundings were targeted every night. Unfortunately, whenever I returned to Belgrade it was the same thing. My wife told me best just go back and stay right there. Every time I was back in Belgrade there would be a major large-scale air-strike.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]...

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter didn't hear the last part of the answer because counsel overlapped.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: If you need any clarification of that last answer, Mr. Ivetic, the interpreter believes it's not all translated.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Well, my recollection of the B/C/S comports with what's on the English. I think it's a completed thought and I think we get the gist of the witness's answer to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: So, sir, I'd like to move on to another event that I believe you have some personal knowledge on relating to -- do you recall the NATO bombing of a civilian bus I believe also in April of 1999 on its way to Podujevo?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN ANDJELKOVIC
utterances.text: I don't remember if this occurred in April. It might have been in May, the 1st of May, perhaps. I think I stayed until the 1st of May. This was usually the time I went back to Belgrade. I had breakfast with the Temporary Executive Council, and after the air-strikes, after the bombing, all of the Executive Council were there, including me. This caused a huge number of casualties. This was a horrendous incident leaving 70 civilians killed. On this bus moving from Pristina to Podujevo there was Serbs and Albanians alike on that bus, I'm certain. Unfortunately, this image will remain etched in my memory forever. It's difficult to describe what we saw. There were bits of bodies, body parts lying all over the place, children killed, bodies ablaze, that sort of thing, a horrendous image.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And, sir, am I correct that when you arrived at the scene you found that the victims of the strike were being rendered first aid and assistance by members of the police, including high-ranking police officials such as General Stevanovic, who was present?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN ANDJELKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. When I came I saw General Stevanovic, and of course the police were there. The first aid people were there from Pristina. Everything was being done that was within their power, and they were trying to take people to hospital so that those who could still be helped were helped.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Just a few more questions and I'd like to move on to the work of the Temporary Executive Council. Am I correct that during the NATO bombing, rather than dealing or seeing any MUP generals frequently, such as Generals Lukic, Djordjevic, or Stevanovic, you saw lower-ranking police officers, for instance, I would direct your attention to the commission that you formed on cooperation and coordination of civilian activities in April of 1999, April 19th, wherein a Blagoje Pesic was the sole MUP participant. Does that accurately reflect the interactions that the Temporary Executive Council had with members of the MUP in the period following the commencement of the bombings?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN ANDJELKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, it was our desire to do everything within our power amid this destruction and war to prevent looting, all those of us whose job it was to do so. Unfortunately, there is looting in every war. There was a commission that was set up to do just that, needless to say, and also took care of the supplies. I know that there was a humanitarian aid mission that arrived from Greece. I think it was brought by the Greek ambassador and there was a shipment of olives --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Could you try to answer the question, please, which is about your contacts with MUP personnel during the war. Could you try to help us with that. Because it's very distracting when you go on to other things that don't have anything to do with the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Perhaps I could ask a more direct question, Your Honour, and might help us if I can catch up with the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir -- I apologise, I've been told that the B/C/S translation also is needing time to catch up with us, so that's why I paused again. Sir, if I can be more concrete, apart from the meeting of the Temporary Executive Council of March 24th, 1999, wherein Generals Lukic and Obrad Stevanovic were present, am I correct that for the duration of the war you rarely saw or dealt with generals in the MUP in your official capacity at the Temporary Executive Council?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN ANDJELKOVIC
utterances.text: On the 24th of March there was a meeting after the state of emergency had been declared and following the meeting of the Serbian National Assembly. When the meeting was scheduled and having discussed this with members of the Temporary Executive Council, they said that representatives of the security forces should be called to the meeting so that they might explain and say what the predictions were, if there would be bombing or not, which is precisely what an organ like that should do in a state of war. In addition to that at all the lower levels about humanitarian aid, about cooperation, I don't think I saw any of them. I may have spoken on the phone to General Lukic twice, perhaps three times, and I only saw him sometime towards the end of the war but I never saw any military men at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. I think -- okay. Thank you very much for your testimony today, Mr. Andjelkovic. I apologise for any confusion or difficulties posed by my questioning.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I think I've got probably questions that I wanted to get finished, Your Honours, so I would pass the witness I guess to the other side.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ivetic. You will now be cross-examined by the Prosecutor, Mr. Stamp. Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Andjelkovic.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN ANDJELKOVIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon. Good afternoon, Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Let's just talk about the statement that you gave or the interview that you gave. That was in 2003, was it, when you were interviewed?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN ANDJELKOVIC
utterances.text: In 2003, in November 2003, I had a 15-minute-long interview, but the proper interview was on the 7th and 8th of February, 2004, if I'm not mistaken.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: It was in 2003, 7th and 8th of February, 2003, was it?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN ANDJELKOVIC
utterances.text: Then this other one was in 2002, maybe I got the year wrong, but I know it was February, 7th and 8th of February.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: The interview in February, Mr. Curtis and Ms. Murtagh were the interviewers?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN ANDJELKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. Marina was taking notes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Marina was the interpreter?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN ANDJELKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, and she was also typing on the PC.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I see. Now, you told them at the end of it all, that's on the 8th, that you didn't want this statement to be given to anybody by the ICTY?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN ANDJELKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And you -- do you recall that for many -- that over long period -- well, I put the question. Do you recall ever receiving any phone calls from anybody at ICTY asking for your permission to disclose the statement -- this statement you gave to them, to the Defence in this case?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN ANDJELKOVIC
utterances.text: No, certainly not.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Do you recall hearing the expression "Joint Command" being used in 1998 or in 1999?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN ANDJELKOVIC
utterances.text: I said a moment ago that during September and the few meetings we had in October, I heard various military terms used and Joint Command perhaps in October, IKM as well of the 3rd Army in Pristina, and headquarters and commands and corps, I did hear those terms but I never gave them any thought.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I'm just asking you about Joint Command. So you say you heard Joint Command being used in 1998?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN ANDJELKOVIC
utterances.text: In 1998 I said that I may have heard someone use the term Joint Command as one of the terms that I heard being used. I don't remember hearing it or using it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You attended --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I'd like the witness to be shown P1468. Perhaps we could hand a hard copy of this document to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: It's a photocopy you have there of a document entitled: "Meetings of the Joint Command for Kosovo and Metohija." And -- and if you open it you'll see that it records various meetings. Have you seen this document before?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN ANDJELKOVIC
utterances.text: I saw it on the 8th of February when Mr. Curtis - I don't know if I pronounce it correctly - showed it to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Have you seen it since then, apart from today of course?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN ANDJELKOVIC
utterances.text: I saw it in this way that you showed it to me and then Mr. Curtis read out several of my statements.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Okay. But the -- when Mr. Curtis showed it to you on the 8th of February, was it the first time you saw it or had you seen it before that?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN ANDJELKOVIC
utterances.text: I saw it for the first time then and that is what I told Mr. Curtis.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Can you look at the second page of that document, please. It refers to a meeting of the 22nd of June, 1998, and it lists the participants, including yourself.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN ANDJELKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And it goes on to October 1990 -- the 20th of October, 1998, where it records many meetings involving these participants. Now, do you recall -- you recall attending meetings frequently in that period with these persons in Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN ANDJELKOVIC
utterances.text: With these and others, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Do you recall attending these meetings at the Executive Council building on many evenings in Kosovo in 1998 in that same period, I'm talking about July to October?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN ANDJELKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, but that building was the building of the Assembly until the 20th of September, and then it was known as the building of the Temporary Executive Council.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thanks.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN ANDJELKOVIC
utterances.text: To -- for precision sake, this building ...

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: What did you call this group of people meeting?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN ANDJELKOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Minic, Mr. Matkovic, and myself, we called it meetings with the security forces, with the army and the police, just as we had meetings with town mayors, with presidents of municipalities, meetings with general managers of companies without any agenda or any form.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thanks. The question was really just what you called it. What did the members of the security forces call it, do you know?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN ANDJELKOVIC
utterances.text: I thought they called it meetings with politicians or -- but certainly not like this.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: No, you said -- but did you hear them referring to these meetings and giving it a name?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN ANDJELKOVIC
utterances.text: No, I didn't hear them mention these meetings specifically, but I heard some of the terms that they used.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Who convened these meetings?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN ANDJELKOVIC
utterances.text: Believe me, they took place as a result of needs to communicate about what was going on on the ground. We gathered during the news cast and to discuss events. Also the office of the Main Board of the SPS was there. This used to be the office of the president of the Assembly. There was another office which used to be occupied by the president of the Executive Council -- I'm sorry. So Mr. Milosavljevic was sitting above me on the floor above me, and as there was no Assembly, that is where we would gather.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well. But when you gathered, who convened the meetings, who invited you to these meetings or did you invite people to these meetings?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN ANDJELKOVIC
utterances.text: Any one of the members of the party, maybe Minic would say, Let's go and talk to the army and the police. I didn't get any formal invitation or a telephone call. We would simply gather when we finished an operative task, Mr. Minic, Matkovic, and myself, to exchange views as to what we had done that day and then we would go to the meeting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Are you indicating that the army -- senior members of the army and the police were just -- just happened to be available whenever you wanted them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, that's not what I'm indicating. I really didn't go into that. I did the tasks that I was given as a member of the Working Group. I wasn't interested in who was calling who. I know that Minic, who was head of the Working Group, would inform me that we would be going to meet the army or the police; that was the extent of what I knew.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So did he organise the meetings?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I really don't believe that he did. He never said explicitly that he was organising meetings. This was never discussed. Sometimes the need arose for us to meet. Sometimes he would say, Let's go and see the mayor. There was no particular pattern or form to it as in someone calling someone else. It was based on what the situation required. That's how we would meet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: This passage started with you saying that: "Any one of the members of the party, maybe Minic, would say, Let's go and talk to the army and the police ... " And it just sounds such a casual arrangement for non-arrangement, for that matter, and gives the impression that senior military figures would be gathering somewhere that you would know they were at and you'd just be able to pop in and see them. Now, I'm having difficulty with that idea, I have to emphasise to you. So if you can help us, please do.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I never said any one of the members of the party; I said the three of us, Minic, Matkovic, and I, who were members of the Working Group. We were appointed and dispatched down there to help stabilise the political situation in Kosovo above all. Sometimes it was necessary if we were to find out that those from Pec would be going through Raus to Pristina for a road to be cleared so that we could see them. I was spending most of my time on the ground and sometimes we would meet in the afternoon to exchange opinions within the Executive Council. That's how it began. I really don't know who scheduled that first meeting, who called that first meeting, but we would go to the Kosovo Assembly premises and meet there. I think this was because none of us were eager to go to police and military premises and thereby create problems for ourselves or for them by simply turning up on the premises belonging to the security forces.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Did you keep a record of the meetings?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, certainly not. We all took notes, each and every one of us, on whatever we needed. I'm quite clumsy myself. I use slips of paper and I tend to misplace them or lose them. All my friends are making jokes at my expense about that. Each of us, whenever necessary, made notes in our own notebooks that we kept on us. I'm certain that no one took minutes, formal minutes, in the sense of Pera or Mika being in charge of the minutes and then the next day you adopt these minutes, that sort of thing. As to whether those present took notes -- well, for example, I would write down some something that I heard so that I could raise further questions, but if I was to say something to a municipality president, for example, I'm on my way to Orahovac to talk to 50 of those whose members of family have been kidnapped and I was there to tell them the police were doing something about it and sometimes when I had no information at all I was on my way there to bear the brunt of the fury of those people there. They would say, do you know anything about them? I said, no, I know nothing. They say, well, why are you here then? Well, I was better off going there trying to talk to those people than no one at all turning up. They needed to be told that measures were being taken and that something was being done.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: If something was happening, if there were meetings that somehow or other were out with the normal state structures, it wouldn't be surprising that there was no formal minute being kept. So please bear in mind when you're trying to assist us that it may not be a particularly surprising situation we're trying to deal with. We don't know. We're just, I suppose, groping a bit in the dark at the moment because there is this document before us and there's lots of people coming denying the existence of the Joint Command, but then having some difficulty in explaining or giving us answers to questions that we think are obvious ones to ask. But the witnesses don't seem to think that. So we are struggling to understand this situation, especially when the Joint Command is clearly referred to in the document and the words are recollected vaguely by the witnesses. Now, can you help us at all about how it was you came to have what appeared to be a fairly regular arrangement for meeting more or less the same people to deal with what clearly was a very, very difficult situation. You don't need to keep telling us how difficult it was. The world knows that and we've had it clearly spelled out to us by everybody here. What we would rather do is concentrate on the detail inquiry into this document. Now, can you help us on how this general meeting -- arrangement for meetings was actually set up?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: I would just further argument this because the type of arrangements which we are hearing appears as if it was a club of friends would like to, all right, let's get together, we go out, we go to this place and solve this problem, and on the other hand, you're also calling the army people in it and so on and deciding things. So this appears to be confusing at least myself. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I never for a minute challenge the fact that we would meet at about 7.30 in the evening in that room. I can't quite know for sure how our first meeting materialised, but the fact of the matter is we met almost every meeting until the end of September. Some of those who were still around in October met and exchanged opinions. This was no standardised sort of meeting. People came from Belgrade, some people came, those who came to the corps or to the police and then some higher-ranking officials came and that's where they would go because that was a place where we would gather. Most of us were outside Pristina and in a situation of crisis if you go to a cafe you have a drink with anyone. The next day, the next thing you know, you're under attack because there was division among the Serbs, too. The next day they're asking why you had a drink with this man and not with that man. So we avoided having drinks outside of these official meetings, for example, with people who held some positions such as the municipality president, someone from the security forces, and so on and so forth. I'm telling you what I saw at the time. Even if someone said the Joint Command at the time, I would have thought there must be something between the police and the army, joint headquarters, joint staff, IKM, IKL, 3rd Army, Pristina from Nis, but it meant nothing at all to me at the time. I'm trying to understand what IKM means now, but at the time it really meant nothing to me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And what do you say it means now?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] IKM, forward command post of the 3rd Army in Pristina, and the headquarters of the 3rd Army is in Nis.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Is this a convenient place to interrupt, Mr. Stamp?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Andjelkovic, we need to break now for 20 minutes, so could you please again leave the courtroom with the usher.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We shall resume at 6.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, there's one thing that needs to be corrected in the transcript. I don't know if we could do that while we're waiting for the witness to save time or I can perhaps say what I heard and then have you confirm with the witness. At page 66, line 7, the acronym IKM is translated as being first and foremost of the 3rd army in Pristina. Listening to the live feed, as I was, I heard him say the term in Serbian, which to me means forward command post, but we can verify that with the witness if need be. It's just I think--

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That is what I heard on the --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. I wasn't sure if it came through on the translation or not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And it's one of these I'm sure will be corrected once it's reviewed overnight.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: No, no, it's important and therefore you have nothing to apologise for. Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Your Honours, I think -- well, it has come to my attention that I am heading to go over time if we abide by the 40 minutes that Mr. Fila spent. He had indicated that this examination-in-chief will be four hours. Now, I don't propose to take even close to four hours, but I respectfully request that I not be held to the time which Mr. Fila took in chief, which I understand --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, we think that you should make an efficient use of the equivalent time. Indeed, we're happy that you would go on to about quarter to and then we'll review the position and see how much re-examination Mr. Fila has at that stage but there doesn't seem to us any reason why we can't get through this witness's evidence today, and so let's go.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You have in front of you a document entitled: "Meetings of the Joint Command of Kosovo and Metohija." You said that looking at the participants at the meeting on page 2, you referred to it as a meeting with the Security Council -- sorry, with the members of the Security Council --

utterances.speaker: ZORAN ANDJELKOVIC
utterances.text: With the forces of security, not council.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes, thank you. Can you just quickly have a look at page 5 of this document. This is page 6 in the English version and page 5 your copy. Do you see where it says 20 -- meeting of the Joint Command for Kosovo and Metohija, 23rd of July, 1998, 2000 to 2300 hours, all members present, including Mr. Matkovic. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN ANDJELKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Did you have a quorum -- this meeting with the security forces that you regularly had, was there a quorum to this meeting or --

utterances.speaker: ZORAN ANDJELKOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I said that there were people who would come once, five times or three times. There was absolutely no one who would say these people have to come and then they are the quorum. It's impossible to say what the quorum would be, it has to be the quorum of something and --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thanks --

utterances.speaker: ZORAN ANDJELKOVIC
utterances.text: -- The number was variable.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The answer -- your answer I think was no. The -- you'll see that the persons attending are described as members, they are described as members, and if this document is genuine, then somebody making these notes thought there was a body of which there was a membership.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, for the two or three days that I was waiting for the beginning of my testimony, I had occasion to look through these documents. And I saw that those absent are usually indicated as members of the Working Group of the Socialist Party of Serbia, but then I saw that there was a Mr. Markovic. He came to Kosovo once. He was not head of the security service. Mr. Stevanovic, Mr. Djordjevic, Mr. Samardzic, commander of the 3rd Army. I told you quite sincerely, people would come who were coming along their chain of command, the Ministry of the Interior, or in the army and us who were politicians and we would see one another in the evenings --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- so one can't talk about a certain number of people present.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: In other words, and you can just tell me yes or no, you cannot assist us by explaining what it means when it says "all members present," and I stress the word "members." You can't help us with that? You don't know what that means?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN ANDJELKOVIC
utterances.text: No, impossible.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN ANDJELKOVIC
utterances.text: I cannot help.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Can you look at page 18 of your document, please, it is page 24 in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Mr. Andjelkovic, if you look at your document you will see there are some printed numbers. Look for the number K00228429 and they are in consecutive order. Have you found that?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN ANDJELKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, I found it, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: The document records -- and if I just go back a page or two, this is a meeting of the 28th of July, 1998, and you see it records you as saying that 52.260 rifles have been distributed. You see that, do you see that, yes or no, let's just start --

utterances.speaker: ZORAN ANDJELKOVIC
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Now --

utterances.speaker: ZORAN ANDJELKOVIC
utterances.text: When -- I'm reported to have said that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Did you say that? Did you say that at any time?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN ANDJELKOVIC
utterances.text: Before this meeting I see Mr. Rade Markovic. He spoke before me. He's General Rade Markovic, but he wasn't a general then. I think he was head of the state security for Belgrade and he was in Prizren on that day. I think he may have attended once or twice only; that's what I said a moment ago. As for what I said, Mr. Stamp, look at the first line, it says: "Supply of the population." Could -- I can't read this properly. It says: "Mr. Rade" here, so could you please put the passage with me as the speaker on the screen. I don't see on the screen what Mr. Stamp is asking me about. It says here "Mr. Rade" here on my screen, who wasn't a general then. He was just Mr. Rade.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Can you go to the next page, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can I comment on my statement? As it's not on the screen, I have it in hard copy. May I answer the question put to me, Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Stamp, what is it we are looking at?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: We are looking at page 24 of the English version --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: -- in the middle of the page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And is the right Serb version on the screen?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: If you can --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Have you not got these all organised to move efficiently --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I found it, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Very well, very well, you can continue and explain it for us. I think that's what you are being asked -- well, no. You were only asked if you had seen that reference and you have, so Mr. Stamp will now ask you another question. Just wait for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You refer here to the distribution of 52.260 rifles. That's what I'm asking you about.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN ANDJELKOVIC
utterances.text: In the first line I'm talking about supplying the people with humanitarian aid, and in the second line I say that this question of supplying the population has to be under full control of all inspections, market inspection, financial police, and all the other that would control supplying the population. This is because the state had organised supplies for the population because what the state was providing, for instance, oil --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Just deal with the point.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Explain the rifles. We can read what it says about humanitarian aid. Just tell us about the rifles. What do you have to say about that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before a session of the government I asked Mr. Vlajko Stojiljkovic how the Ministry of the Interior is going to resolve the problem of defence of non-Albanian villages who were under constant attack. He told me that the Ministry of the Interior had formed 200 reserve police detachments with 5.000 [as interpreted] people. I didn't believe it. I asked the question. Everybody was laughing because everybody knew that Mr. Vlajko Stojiljkovic is prone to exaggerate, that he likes to say what Mr. Milosevic likes to hear rather than what is on the ground. I spoke about this once more with Mr. Vlajko Stojiljkovic and he said, What they're saying over there has nothing to do with reality. I have made a decision and I have discussed that at meetings of the party and I conveyed this to Mr. Curtis during the interview.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I am none the wiser about what this reference is to 52.260 rifles. Can you help me with that. I don't know what you're saying about it. Mr. Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I may, Your Honour, a correction which may be of assistance in understanding what the witness is saying. Line 8, page 72, he mentioned 52.000 people and here it says 5.000. So maybe that will clarify what he's trying to say.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So let me repeat, Your Honour: The minister of the police, Mr. Vlajko Stojiljkovic, I asked while we were waiting for a meeting of the government to start, I asked him, Mr. Minister, how are you going to protect the villages in Kosovo who are under constant attack by the KLA? And he said the Ministry of the Interior had decided to set up 200 police detachments with 52.260 reservists. I didn't believe that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, I know that, but what's the rifles got to do with this? What happened with rifles?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 52.000 reservists surely need to have rifles --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- if they are a reserve police detachment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I understand that. Did they get them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At that meeting, representatives of the police from Pristina laughed at the position of Mr. Vlajko Stojiljkovic. How -- whether they got them or --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes or no?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, that's even better, I don't know, that's another simple answer you can give. Please help us with the specific questions you're being asked. That has taken ages and now we'll have to extend, no doubt, the time that's available for this cross-examination because you're not listening to the instructions you're being given. Now, please. Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You were involved -- yes, yes. You were involved -- or the TEC at some point in time was involved in creating local village defence forces?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN ANDJELKOVIC
utterances.text: Not took part in the formation, but suggested and proposed that local security be formed. This is not the same as security. This has to do with the municipalities and not with the Ministry of the Interior.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Could you have a look at page 39 of that document, and in English it's 49. If you look for the page with K0228450.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN ANDJELKOVIC
utterances.text: [In English] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: That's a meeting you will see there on the 12th of August, 1998. If you could look to where it says that Mr. Minic speaks.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN ANDJELKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I see it, but could you please read it and I get the interpretation. I really am unable to read the handwriting.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: It says there - and in English we are on page 50, I beg your pardon. It says: "Collection of weapons continue." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN ANDJELKOVIC
utterances.text: Which line is it?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: That is at the bottom of the page marked K0228450.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN ANDJELKOVIC
utterances.text: Very well, "kuplje," [phoen] I believe that's what it says, I believe you, but I can't read it. The lasting line probably.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What's your question, Mr. Stamp?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And you see further on Mr. Sainovic, if you look further down on the document or on the next page, you see Mr. Sainovic speaking and he says: "DB are to cover and take over the third area" and he also says: "Confiscation of weapons process to be reinforced." Do you see that in your documents where Mr. Sainovic speaks?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN ANDJELKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do see that Mr. Sainovic is speaking. I don't know which line you're referring to.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: If you look at your document K0228451, do you have that in front of you -- or maybe could we just use e-court, e-court page 40, of the B/C/S version. Mr. Andjelkovic, I'll ask you to use the screen, the computer screen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Fila.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I appreciate the effort of Mr. Stamp. He read out incorrectly a moment ago. Now he's using the word "confiscation," but no one could see it. Could it be enlarged, please, and only once it's enlarged can the witness be asked to answer because we can't see that. Maybe it does say "confiscated," but we can't see it. Could it be enlarged, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That's being done, Mr. --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Immediately under -- yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Could you read that to us, please, Mr. Andjelkovic.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN ANDJELKOVIC
utterances.text: "That the DB should apply this third zone," if that's what you're asking me about. Could you please read it for me. I'm sorry. I can't read it. You may consider me illiterate but I really can't read it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Do you see where Mr. Sainovic says that the confiscation of weapons process is to be reinforced?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN ANDJELKOVIC
utterances.text: I believe that's what -- I believe you if you say that's what it says.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Objection, I'm sorry, I really can't see that anywhere. Will you read it out in English, please, Mr. Stamp, please, I'm not reproaching you in any sense. I can't see it in Serbian.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Fila, he has read it in English and that's from a translation. Now, the witness apparently cannot read what's on the screen because it's -- of the way it's written. So we'll proceed on the basis that Mr. Stamp has got it right and see if the witness can assist, and parties can assist us in due course about what exactly is said there and his questions will be a complete and utter waste of time if it's shown that the word "confiscate" isn't there.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may --

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It says "konsoliduje," third line.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]...

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Third line, that it should be "consolidated" and not "confiscated." You can see that yourself --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Please just be quiet for the moment until we sort out what this is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: My understanding, Mr. Fila, is that Mr. Stamp is referring to the last line -- oh --

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He's talking about the third line from the top and the word is "konsoliduje," that it should be consolidated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... last section. Mr. Andjelkovic, what does the second-last line say under "Sainovic," the second-last one?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I can read it properly, is it to increase or to strengthen administrative -- no, I'm sorry, I really can't read it. Your Honour, I'm being quite sincere about it. I have borrowed these glasses, that's true.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, can this word be enlarged, please. And you will see that the first letter is A and not K. It's "administrative." The handwriting is very terrible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Stamp, is there a typewritten B/C/S version of this document?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Andjelkovic, can you read it any better now, the second-last line?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. If I'm reading it correctly, it's to increase or something across the administrative line, but I don't know what. Across the administrative line, but what, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, there you have no basis for your question, Mr. Stamp, so let's move to something else.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: There's one last question on this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Could we go to page 153 of the B/C/S version on e-court and it's page 158 in English.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What date is it, Mr. Stamp, for me to find it more quickly?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: It's the 28th of October. Can we just --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: If you put it on the screen as well.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have the 26th and the 29th on me, 26th and then the 29th. I don't have the 28th.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Can you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: This is the very last page, is it, Mr. Stamp, in the e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: No, it's not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, it is on ours, I think. Have you got the right number?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Page number 161, and I have page 143 in e-court, 143 in the B/C/S e-court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, you've just asked us to go to pages in the 150s; you're now changing that. Can we not have some planning and organisation in the way that this is being conducted because it's not really helping us very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well. Let me confer on the matter. Page 143 in e-court is K0228554 --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is the 26th.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes. That is what I indicated, the 26th.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And in the English version for Your Honours, that is page 158.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Just so that the witness realises that we don't overlook detail, you actually talked about the 28th, but that's been corrected now.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's what I heard.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You see that meeting there of the 26th?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN ANDJELKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And Mr. Sainovic is present at that meeting. Now, I'd like us to go to page 160 of the English, which is 145 of your copy in e-court.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN ANDJELKOVIC
utterances.text: Which date?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: The same date but it's -- we're now at page 145, that's K0228556. Do you see Mr. Sainovic there speaking about what he told or what he spoke to about -- what he spoke to Ambassador Hill about, is that where you are?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN ANDJELKOVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, 526, that's not consistent with this page. There is probably a page missing.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Page 556.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN ANDJELKOVIC
utterances.text: Oh, 556, this is 526. There it is, 556. Yes, please, go ahead. I've found it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You see Mr. Sainovic speaking about the --

utterances.speaker: ZORAN ANDJELKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: -- meeting with Ambassador Hill?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN ANDJELKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. When I -- Ambassador Hill that we are working on --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: No, no, just -- I wish to take you to a particular part. He's speaking about a discussion he had with Ambassador Hill and you see it goes on and he says: "It is necessary for all to inform themselves about DTS activities in the field." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN ANDJELKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: What are DTS activities, can you just tell us quickly and briefly in a sentence if you can?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN ANDJELKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, based on my understanding, this is sabotage and terrorist forces, sabotage and terrorist forces. I'm not sure whether or not the expansion might be, it might not be that, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: It also says: "When pulling out you must be careful not to let anyone find out that parts of some detachments did not pull out. There must not be any discrepancies with information that was given." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN ANDJELKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Now, my question is simply this: Having regard to those passages I showed you, would you agree with me or would you not agree with me that Mr. Sainovic on occasion gave instructions at these meetings?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN ANDJELKOVIC
utterances.text: At the time he was president of the commission for cooperation with the OSCE. It was necessary for the Milosevic-Holbrooke Agreement to be fully implemented in terms of the number of people envisaged by that agreement. The agreement exactly envisaged how many policemen, how many soldiers in Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes. And what I'm asking is does the passage I'm speaking about we just went over, does that indicate to you that Mr. Sainovic was in a position to give instructions at these meetings?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN ANDJELKOVIC
utterances.text: These are not instructions. He was president of the commission for cooperation with the OSCE. It is the task of the commission to comply with that agreement. The state had an interest in seeing the Milosevic-Holbrooke Agreement fully implemented.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Do you know what -- well, do you know what he meant when he said that "You must be careful not to let anyone find out that parts of some detachments did not pull out. There must not be discrepancies with the information already given"?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN ANDJELKOVIC
utterances.text: Information already given on the number of policemen and soldiers necessary and this has to tally with the situation on the ground. This is a sort of warning or request, if you like, what the state has signed must now be implemented or at least that is my reading.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Were there some detachments that did not pull out in accordance with the agreement?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN ANDJELKOVIC
utterances.text: I'd be hard-put to answer that. I know little about military and police business and I was not a member of the commission for the implementation of this agreement. I was only concerned with the work of the Temporary Executive Council.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well. Do you recall being shown that passage by Mr. Curtis when he interviewed you?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN ANDJELKOVIC
utterances.text: No, not this one.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Do you not recall telling Mr. Curtis that where Mr. Sainovic says: "When pulling out we must be careful enough not to allow anyone to find out that parts of some detachments did not pull out. There must not be any discrepancies with information already given," did you tell Mr. Curtis in respect to that that if that is what happened then there was a breach of the agreement?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN ANDJELKOVIC
utterances.text: I'm still saying just that. If someone failed to pull out based on the agreement and that would constitute a violation of the agreement, but I'm not saying this was actually the case. I'm still saying the same thing, if there was a unit or a policeman who outstayed the time envisaged in the agreement, well, that's only logical. I think that's what Mr. Sainovic is doing here. He is sending out a warning that no such thing should happen. That is my understanding.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: If you look further on that document - and now we move to page 161 of the English version and I think it is at page 160 -- or, sorry, 146 of your version --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Which is the next page.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Mr. Andjelkovic says: "Nobody is authorised to take away our documents. All the documents are to be kept on the Joint Command premises." Did you say that?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN ANDJELKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Did you say that?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN ANDJELKOVIC
utterances.text: Certainly not like this, but there are two statements that I made on this same page. It's something that I saw as I was going through these documents. One is entirely inaccurate. Whenever I called the Albanians Siptars, all those who know me, both Albanians and Serbs, know that I would never say anything like that. I had a member of the Temporary Executive Council replaced because he did not agree with me that Albanians and Turks and so on and so forth should be called members of ethnic communities, not even ethnic minorities, and there is this insinuation being made in these documents to the effect that I called the Albanians Siptars. This is just not true, this is an outrage both against me and against my Albanian friends, people that I still see on a regular basis. For example, the first thing being said in this document quotes me as saying just so as to avoid that previous members of the police force should remain in the reserve police force. Your Honour -- and I gave Mr. Curtis my book, it's only about information. I don't like to write things post facto but this other book --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Let's try and concentrate -- are you saying that for you to refer to an --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [Previous translation continues]... understand you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Are you saying that for you to refer to an Albanian by the use of the word "Siptar" is offensive?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, in my opinion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Is that what you understand to be the position among --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I never pronounced that word. I never uttered that word.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Do you understand that to be the position among Serbs in general?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Those I consider my friends don't call the Albanians Siptars, although sometimes the term is used, but they're normally referred to members of the Albanian ethnic minority or ethnic community, but I have a large number of friends and I don't like to see something like this turning up in a document and attributed to me as a quote. I'm not saying it's necessarily derogatory; what I'm saying it that it is certainly not a term that I would use.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Why wouldn't you use it if it's not derogatory?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just because my Albanian friends, those who were my colleagues in the youth centre and in the centre for tolerance, I'd prefer to call them Albanians. And in my capacity as a politician, I never used the term differently. Definitely wherever you see the word "Siptar" being used and attributed to me, you can be certain of one thing: I never used it. I still see my friends from Pristina once a week over in Belgrade, Albanian friends, and I don't like that term being used.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Bearing in mind the personnel who were attending these meetings, are you surprised to see the word "Siptar" written in this document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, in relation to politicians and in relation to most present there, with the exception, obviously, of the person taking the notes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As for Mr. Stamp's question, at the meeting Mr. Pavkovic - and Mr. Pavkovic attended the meeting - he said at the end of the meeting that General Samardzic, who was the commander of the 3rd Army, his superior at the time, had told him to not go there again or meet any civilians. Of course he was perfectly within his rights. This is the military chain of command. Let's imagine Mr. Vlajko Stojiljkovic had ordered a policeman not to be there, he would have been perfectly within his rights. We were civilians and we did not intervene with these things --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Andjelkovic.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN ANDJELKOVIC
utterances.text: I'm just answering your question, Mr. Stamp. But likewise, I'm in that office, I had been there for three weeks, I'm the president of the Temporary Executive Council, nobody has the right to ask for my documents from that office, documents I received, dozens of pages. I don't like civilians interfering in the work of the army and the same thing applies vice versa, the army searching my own office. Everything that remained in that office alongside Mr. De Mello and his representatives when they found a different office for us when I stayed in Pristina until October 2000 with the members of the temporary Executive Board, they took all the documents and you probably have it, what was there and what was searched and what was taken. Therefore when I said --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I have turned off your microphone because you are way past answering the question you were asked. Mr. Stamp, your next question.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Well, the --

utterances.speaker: ZORAN ANDJELKOVIC
utterances.text: Okay, so, I did not mention the Joint Command, that much is certain, but the documents, my documents from my office, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: But did you recommend that documents were to be kept somewhere?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN ANDJELKOVIC
utterances.text: I said everyone should keep their documents in their own office, the military in their own, the police in their own, and I kept mine in the Temporary Executive Council. I had already held up until that point in time four meetings of the Temporary Executive Council.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Can we have a look at page 2166 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Where are you --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: -- with your cross-examination, Mr. Stamp?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I'm moving very slowly and I think I have at least a half-hour left, if I'd be granted that period of time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I know that you've been interrupted from time to time, but that's largely because it's a fairly ill-prepared exercise that you're going through. You must get through this more quickly if you want to ask a reasonable number of questions, having regard to the time that's available to us overall and bearing in mind the efficiency with which the Defence are conducting their examinations. Now, this is important -- an important area and we are not inclined to stop you just at the moment because of the interruptions, but you're going to have to pay back this time at some stage soon and Mr. Hannis made it clear -- he indicated yesterday that the cross-examination wouldn't be this length. So you're doing something different from what we anticipated, but please continue and try to make it as efficient as possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Mr. --

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I won't have any additional questions; therefore, if Mr. Stamp can wrap this up in 15 minutes, we're going to be all right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: He's just said he's got at least half an hour, so let's move on, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Let's move to 2166. P2166, could we get that document for the witness, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: If you see the front page of that document it's entitled: "The minutes of the meeting of the operations interdepartmental staff of the suppression of terrorism in Kosovo and Metohija." Have you seen this document before or a document like this before?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN ANDJELKOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: It is a record of a meeting on the 29th of October, 1998, chaired by President Milutinovic in which, if you can -- sorry, President Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: If you can see from the first page that you are one of the participants at that meeting?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN ANDJELKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Could we look at page 10 in your version, please, and this is page 9 of the English version, page 10 in the B/C/S copy, please. At the top of page 10 on your version - and this is the bottom of page 9 - do you see there Mr. Milomir Minic proposed the following and at item 2 it says that the question of unifying, systemizing and safe-guarding documentation concerning the activities of state organs in suppressing terrorism in Kosovo and Metohija should be resolved" --

utterances.speaker: ZORAN ANDJELKOVIC
utterances.text: All right. I don't understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I will ask the question. And prior to that, in item 1 he refers to the operation staff providing an assessment of how successful is the Joint Command for KiM has conferred the authorisations conferred upon him. Do you recall him referring at that meeting to the Joint Command?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN ANDJELKOVIC
utterances.text: No, I don't, he spoke about political issues and this is the last meeting at which we as a Working Group were with Slobodan Milosevic. The last time I was there was on the 16th of October, 2000, that was the next time.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Do you recall him or anybody else at that meeting - and I just -- to move quickly, I just represent to you that this record has various persons at the meeting including Mr. Sainovic, Mr. Milutinovic, Mr. Milosevic, referring to the Joint Command --

utterances.speaker: ZORAN ANDJELKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I remember the meeting, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Do you recall anybody at that meeting referring to the Joint Command?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN ANDJELKOVIC
utterances.text: Let me be sincere, Your Honours. I wasn't listening to those terms. I wasn't interested. I listened to Mr. Minic talk about the political situation in Kosovo and Metohija. I was interested in that. As for the rest that they were saying, I just wasn't interested. I was there to see the president of the socialist party of Serbia and Mr. Minic informed me that we would be seeing the president. I had no idea who would be at that meeting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You are -- what position did you hold in the party, remind me?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was a member of the Main Board, nothing more, consisting of 350 members. I still have that humble capacity in the party.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And you weren't interested to know what the Joint Command might be with your interest in matters bureaucratic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, as I told you, I may have heard different terms being used at the meeting. I believe them to be military terms. I simply didn't spend any time thinking about who was using which term, and I am being entirely honest.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But here we have one of your Working Group using that expression according to this record, that's why these questions are being asked of you, not because it is a soldier using them.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right. Mr. Stamp --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understand you entirely. I don't know if Mr. Minic used the term or not, really, I am being very honest here.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: If we have a look at page 13, the top of page 13 in the B/C/S version of that and it's -- on the English translation it's on the middle of page 12. It records President Milutinovic saying he supported the proposal for consideration of the continued status of the Joint Command and Milutinovic believes the Joint Command should continue functioning for a while. You see that there?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN ANDJELKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Let's look at page 13, the bottom of page 14 -- page 13 in the B/C/S copy and the middle of page 13 in English. It has Deputy Prime Minister Sainovic agreeing with the opinion that the viability of the continued activity of the Joint Command for Kosovo and Metohija in its present composition should be re-evaluated. He said that the number of people thus engaged should be reduced and better prepare them to be more effective. May I just repeat that. He said that the number of people thus engaged should be reduced and better prepare them for more effective action in new conditions. Okay, I accept that you're saying that you didn't hear about the Joint Command. Did you hear them speaking about any body or group that ought to be reduced or ought to be re-organised in respect to the work in Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN ANDJELKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, about the need for cooperation between the police and the army. They were talking about that all the time, whether this cooperation went by the name of joint staff or Joint Command, as you suggest, is not something that I can say. But I did hear about the need for cooperation between the police and the army under the conditions that prevailed at the time. This was something that was only natural.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well. Let's turn quickly to the meeting you had or you say not a meeting, you say you went to dinner with General Vasiljevic on one occasion. And General Vasiljevic just happened to walk into a situation where -- I'm sorry, I withdraw that. You went to a meeting on one occasion with Mr. Sainovic in June 1999, do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN ANDJELKOVIC
utterances.text: As I said, Mr. Sainovic came to see me --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes, yes, we know that --

utterances.speaker: ZORAN ANDJELKOVIC
utterances.text: -- I was glad -- [In English] Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Do you recall if there were maps in the room where the group were, the group of people were?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN ANDJELKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I remember PCs and right in the middle of that room there was a bowling alley, I think that's what it was. I knew General Vasiljevic's face from TV, his face was familiar, but I had never met him before and there were a number of other generals I didn't recognise.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Do you remember if there were maps in the room?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN ANDJELKOVIC
utterances.text: I don't think, but really I don't remember. I saw the computers and sheets, piles of paper around the computers. The room itself is twice as big as this courtroom; it's a bowling alley, after all.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Did you see General Lukic give a presentation in which he pointed to places on maps? This is what General Vasiljevic told us -- sorry, I beg your pardon. Sorry, I beg your pardon. Did you see General Lazarevic there at that meeting?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN ANDJELKOVIC
utterances.text: I think he was -- well, there were between 10 and 15 people there, perhaps even more --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Did you see General Lazarevic --

utterances.speaker: ZORAN ANDJELKOVIC
utterances.text: -- I think he was there. I don't know who else was there. I can't swear upon it, but he probably was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: But --

utterances.speaker: ZORAN ANDJELKOVIC
utterances.text: -- but as I said, I couldn't swear upon it. 78 days of bombing are committed between Belgrade and Pristina. This one dinner, who was there, I really don't know. I can't swear on it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: What I'm suggesting to you -- or asking you about is whether or not you saw any general describe what was happening in the field by reference to maps in that meeting.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN ANDJELKOVIC
