utterances.text: No. At that dinner what was discussed was whether General Pavkovic or Lazarevic -- they were talking about the border, something like that, that's what I remember, about the border, the attempts to de-block the border by air-strikes so that forces might come in. That's all. But I don't remember anything else. I was glad to see Pavkovic after nearly 70 days.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: When you went into that room, were the generals there, and you say you don't remember who, were they seated around the table?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN ANDJELKOVIC
utterances.text: They were seated around that table and around those computers in the room, some officers, some people.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Now, was the meal served as you went in or did you speak with these people before?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN ANDJELKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, we were having dinner. First we talked and then we had dinner. How long we talked for is not something that I can say, half an hour, 45 minutes, it was a long time ago. I can't remember, but I know that we were having dinner.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well --

utterances.speaker: ZORAN ANDJELKOVIC
utterances.text: That's what I wanted, that's why I was there and to see those people.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Do you recall whether or not Mr. Lukic gave a presentation at that meeting?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN ANDJELKOVIC
utterances.text: I really don't know. I can't remember -- I was interested in hearing what Mr. Sainovic would say about the talks between Milosevic, Ahtissari, Chernomyrdin, because we all wanted this chaos to come to an end as soon as possible. And I know that on the 2nd there was a session of the Executive Council.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You told us, Mr. Andjelkovic, that you were with Mr. Sainovic at your office?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN ANDJELKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's what I said, from my office we went there.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And you were anxious to hear what Mr. Sainovic would say about these meetings when you went there?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN ANDJELKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I asked Mr. Sainovic about the agreement and then I asked whether he would have dinner with us. We had a small coffee bar like everyone, and he said, General Pavkovic has invited us to dinner and I'll speak about the negotiations there, and that's why I wanted to hear what I was going to say.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Now, as -- at that time in June, am I to understand you correctly that you are saying that you could have attended a meeting with generals like General Pavkovic and General Lazarevic and General Lukic and you don't recall whether or not they gave reports?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN ANDJELKOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Stamp, I was president of the Temporary Executive Council and from the minutes of the work of that council you will see that my main concern was to feed the people who were coming back and who were short of food in Kosovo and Metohija. And I asked for aid from Belgrade and Mr. De Mello when he came in May with an inter-parliamentary delegation and there's a note in the UN about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You're saying that having not seen these persons who are engaged in fighting this war for -- since the war started, you attend a meeting where they are present and you cannot recall whether or not they reported about what was happening in the field at this point in time?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN ANDJELKOVIC
utterances.text: I had my own worries and I couldn't help the army and the police. I had problems with members of the Executive Council, and you can see this from the minutes --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well, very well.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN ANDJELKOVIC
utterances.text: -- how to feed the people and how to put an end to this horror in Kosovo and when the agreement would finally be signed and that's what I told Mr. De Mello. When we changed the plan that Zivadin Jovanovic had made for him, we wanted to see as much as possible in Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... you cannot recall whether or not that happened?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Where are you now, Mr. Stamp?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: 15 minute.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: On different topics?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I just -- yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, it won't be tonight, that's ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It was a regular feature of discussions with Defence counsel when they were cross-examining Prosecution witnesses that they should prioritize the cross-examination. You cannot in this arena examine the way you might in a domestic context on every little point that you think you might be able to explore with the witness. There has to be prioritizing. There's no indication in this case that you really have given much thought to that. As with the Defence, however, we are very reluctant to actually stop any cross-examination, but we will stop them if we really think our requests are not being given due recognition. We note that you think this can be completed in 15 minutes tomorrow, and therefore we will allow you 15 minutes tomorrow. I regret, Mr. Andjelkovic, that means you have to come back tomorrow. We were doing all we thought we could to try and complete this evidence today. We will be sitting at 9.00 tomorrow morning. You should be here, ready to resume at 9.00, and overnight you must have absolutely no discussion with anybody whatsoever about the evidence in this case. You can discuss anything else you like but not the evidence in this case. Would you now please leave the courtroom with the usher. Mr. Fila, do you have only one more witness after this?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I want to give you a prognosis. The examination-in-chief will take as long as this one did, and I do only have one more witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Sepenuk, I take it you'll be in a position to start tomorrow?

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, we will.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And if -- how long do you estimate the opening taking?

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: I would say half an hour or so, 45 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So there may also be evidence?

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: There could be, yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you very much. We'll sit tomorrow at 9.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Friday, the 31st day of August, 2007, at 9.00 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 7.09 p.m.,
